subtitle: What do People, Access and Culture mean at DSD? This introduction connects each idea to the everyday decisions made in disability services and explains why that matters.
scope: For employees in any role who want a shared starting point for equity work. The examples concern DSD, but the reasoning can support work throughout DHS.
introTranscript: Diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility are connected ideas with different uses. This course starts with their meaning, follows a practice service notice through design and review, and asks what staff can change within their responsibility. You will examine a barrier, make room for a missing perspective, compare ways to offer access, and choose a small improvement to review later. Work through the six lessons at your own pace, and return to the activities when they are useful. They do not diagnose your beliefs or assign an intercultural orientation. You can return to any lesson when it becomes useful.

lessons.title: Four connected ideas
lessons.summary: Use the four terms to describe different parts of a familiar work situation.
lessons.objective: Distinguish diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility in a meeting example.
objectives: Distinguish diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility in a meeting example.
Identify the difference between inviting people and enabling them to contribute.
Describe one practical improvement without judging a person’s motives.
takeaways: A diverse group can still face unequal opportunities to participate.
Inclusion involves contribution and influence, not attendance alone.
Accessibility belongs in planning rather than being added only after someone struggles.
lessons.statement: A meeting can include different people and still make it difficult for some of them to take part.

image.caption: Planning together offers a chance to examine how a meeting will work for its participants.

intro.heading: Look at the process, not just the invitation
intro.body:
Imagine a practice DSD team that invites analysts, service users, providers, and communications staff to review a new notice. The group contains different experiences. That is a feature of its diversity, but it tells us little about who can read the draft, join the discussion, or influence the final notice. A participant who cannot use the document may be present without having the same opportunity to contribute.

The four ideas help you ask more precise questions. Diversity asks whose experiences are present or absent. Equity asks how the process distributes opportunity and whether avoidable barriers affect people differently. Inclusion asks whether contributions receive attention and can affect the decision. Accessibility asks whether the material and activity are usable by people with disabilities. These questions overlap without becoming interchangeable.

Start with an observable part of the work. You do not need to decide that the organizer is uncaring to notice that the draft was sent too late. A useful conversation names that condition, asks who it affects, and explores a change. Different people may prefer different ways to contribute, so checking with participants is more useful than assuming a single solution.

inThisLesson: Distinguish diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility in a meeting example.
Identify the difference between inviting people and enabling them to contribute.
Describe one practical improvement without judging a person’s motives.
Apply the four terms to a practice review meeting.
lessons.keyStatement: Name the part of the process you can examine or change.

flashcards.back: Differences in people’s experiences, identities, perspectives, and ways of approaching a situation.
Examining and changing barriers so people have a fair opportunity to participate and benefit.
Creating real opportunities to contribute and considering what people contribute.
Making information, spaces, activities, and services usable by people with disabilities.
A condition in a process or environment that makes participation or use harder.
Information that supports an explanation while leaving its limits visible.

accordion.heading: What each idea helps you notice

items.title: Presence
items.body: A participant list can reveal whose experience is represented. It cannot establish whether every person had a fair chance to read, respond, or be heard.

items.title: Opportunity
items.body: Look at the conditions for participation: advance information, usable formats, timing, ways to respond, and clarity about the decision. A barrier can be addressed without guessing someone’s identity or intentions.

items.title: Influence
items.body: Ask what happens after a contribution. A team can acknowledge a suggestion, explain its decision, and show what changed. Agreement with every suggestion is not required for a meaningful response.

tabs.heading: Three descriptions of the same meeting

tabs.label: Attendance
tabs.body: Twelve people attended. This describes an activity. It does not show whether the meeting was accessible or whether different perspectives influenced the draft.

tabs.label: Contribution
tabs.body: Participants could submit comments before, during, or after the discussion. This describes opportunities to contribute. The team still needs to check whether those opportunities worked.

tabs.label: Follow-through
tabs.body: The editor records which suggestions changed the notice and explains why some could not be used. This gives participants a way to see how the review affected the decision.

check.question: Which statement distinguishes inclusion from attendance?
check.correct: The team considers participants’ contributions and explains how they affected the notice.
wrong: Everyone was invited, so everyone was included equally.
The room contained several job titles, so access was guaranteed.
The meeting lasted an hour, so every participant had influence.
check.feedbackCorrect: You connected participation to the decision. Attendance is useful information, but it does not establish that a person’s contribution received consideration.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An invitation, a varied group, and time together describe parts of the meeting. Look for evidence of an opportunity to contribute and a response to that contribution.

items.text: People with different service experiences join the review.
A usable draft is shared in advance.
Written comments are accepted after the meeting.
The editor explains why a suggested change was adopted.
The group includes staff from different teams.
Participants receive a summary of decisions and reasons.

lessons.next: Next, examine a barrier without turning it into an assumption about a person.

scenario.context: A practice review meeting is about to begin. One participant says the document arrived too late to review with their reading support. The organizer says everyone received the same email.
scenario.prompt: What would help the team respond?
options: Acknowledge the timing barrier, ask what would support participation, and arrange a useful way to contribute before the decision.
Explain that identical emails prove the process was fair.
Assume the participant cannot review complex documents and remove them from future invitations.
responses: This addresses the condition and keeps the participant involved. Check what is useful instead of selecting a solution based on an assumption.
Identical delivery does not establish equal opportunity to use the material. The timing concern still needs a response.
The comment concerns this process. It does not justify a conclusion about the person’s ability or removing their opportunity to contribute.

lessons.transfer: Choose a meeting or review you help organize. Which of the four ideas would help you ask a more specific question about it?

move.control: You can clarify the decision and ask how participants prefer to contribute.
move.failure: Counting attendance as proof of inclusion can hide barriers in the process.
move.next: Write one observation about participation and one question to ask before the next review.

lessons.title: Notice a barrier before explaining it
lessons.summary: Separate what you observed from the explanation you first imagined.
lessons.objective: Separate an observation from an assumption in a service-access example.
objectives: Separate an observation from an assumption in a service-access example.
Identify more than one plausible explanation for an incomplete response.
Draft a question that checks the process without blaming the person.
takeaways: A missed response does not explain why the response was missed.
Several conditions can contribute to the same result.
Ask a question that helps you learn what happened.
lessons.statement: A low response rate is a reason to investigate, not a description of people’s interest or ability.

image.caption: Listening can reveal conditions that a response count does not explain.

intro.heading: Begin with what you actually know
intro.body:
In this example, a team sends a notice asking service users to confirm a contact preference. Only half respond. Someone says that people are not interested. That may feel like an explanation, but the team has not established it. The count describes replies received; it does not tell the team whether the notice arrived, made sense, could be used, or offered an acceptable way to respond.

An equity approach makes the uncertainty visible. First describe the observation accurately: half of the notices received a reply within the chosen period. Then list questions about the process. Was the address current? Could people understand the requested action? Was a phone response available? Did the deadline allow enough time? These questions create an investigation rather than an accusation.

A useful question also respects the person answering. Instead of asking why someone failed to comply, you might ask what made it easier or harder to respond. You can offer more than one way to give feedback and avoid collecting personal details that are not needed. The goal is to improve the work, not to assemble a profile of a person’s presumed motivation. Keep explanations provisional until evidence supports them.

inThisLesson: Separate an observation from an assumption in a service-access example.
Identify more than one plausible explanation for an incomplete response.
Draft a question that checks the process without blaming the person.
Rewrite a blaming explanation as a question about the notice.
lessons.keyStatement: An observation tells you what happened; an explanation still needs support.

accordion.heading: Three steps for a fair investigation

items.title: Describe
items.body: State the count, period, and action you measured. Avoid words such as unwilling or careless when the evidence is only a missing response.

items.title: Explore
items.body: Consider the notice, delivery method, timing, response options, and support. Several conditions may overlap. Do not select one explanation simply because it fits your first impression.

items.title: Check
items.body: Ask people about the process and compare their accounts with appropriate records. Do not treat one account as a population-wide conclusion, but do not dismiss it because it is one account.

tabs.label: Judgment
tabs.body: People did not care enough to reply. This claims a motive the count does not establish and gives the team little it can use to improve the notice.

tabs.label: Observation
tabs.body: Twenty of forty recipients replied by Friday. This is clearer, provided the count and delivery list are reliable. It still leaves the reasons open.

tabs.label: Question
tabs.body: What about the wording, delivery, deadline, or response method made it easier or harder to reply? This invites evidence about conditions the team may be able to change.

check.question: What can the team conclude from a 50 percent reply rate alone?
check.correct: Half of the measured recipients replied within the measured period; the reasons need further investigation.
wrong: Half of the recipients were uninterested in services.
People who did not respond lack the skills to use a notice.
The form was inaccessible to every nonrespondent.
check.feedbackCorrect: The conclusion stays within the evidence. You can now investigate possible causes without treating them as established.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Each alternative adds a cause that the count does not show. A barrier is possible, but its presence and effect need to be examined.

sorting.heading: Observation, possible explanation, or next question?

items.text: Twenty replies arrived before Friday.
The response period may have been too short.
Which response options were offered?
Five callers asked what the notice meant.
Some recipients may not have received the notice.
What changed when a clearer notice was tested?

lessons.next: Next, consider differences without making identity-based assumptions.

scenario.context: In this example, a team notices fewer online replies from one geographic area. A colleague concludes that residents there dislike technology. The team has not checked connectivity, delivery, or the available alternatives.
scenario.prompt: Which response keeps the investigation useful?
options: Ask what the data actually measures and examine access conditions before explaining the difference.
Record the colleague’s explanation as a confirmed cultural preference.
Remove the area from the report because the difference is uncomfortable.
responses: You keep the observed difference visible while testing explanations. Geographic patterns do not establish any individual’s preference.
That turns an unsupported interpretation into a group characteristic. It may direct the team toward the wrong response.
Removing the pattern conceals a potentially useful question. Report the limits and investigate rather than hiding the result.

lessons.transfer: Recall a recent assumption about a delayed response. Write what you knew, what you inferred, and one respectful question that could test the inference.

move.control: You can describe evidence accurately and propose a question about the process.
move.failure: A confident explanation can prevent the team from investigating the actual barrier.
move.next: Replace one unsupported explanation in a draft note with an observation and a question.

lessons.title: Make room for different perspectives
lessons.summary: Use curiosity to learn about a person’s experience without treating them as a representative of a whole group.
lessons.objective: Identify when a broad statement hides relevant differences in experience.
objectives: Identify when a broad statement hides relevant differences in experience.
Draft a respectful invitation for an individual perspective.
Choose a way to compare accounts without ranking people’s experiences.
takeaways: Shared goals do not mean everyone experiences the same process.
A person can describe their experience without speaking for a whole community.
Look for differences that matter to the decision.
lessons.statement: “We all want a clear notice” can be a starting point; it is not proof that the notice works in the same way for everyone.

image.caption: Different perspectives can help a team understand what a shared goal requires.

intro.heading: Common purpose, different experiences
intro.body:
The program’s intercultural learning invites movement from overlooking or flattening differences toward recognizing them and adapting practice. In the IDI-related language used here, Minimization can involve overemphasizing shared experiences, while Acceptance and Adaptation make more room for meaningful differences and changes in approach. These are learning concepts, not labels to attach to a coworker. This course does not assess anyone’s orientation.

Consider the practice notice again. The team agrees that every recipient needs a clear explanation. One person prefers a concise written summary; another needs a chance to ask questions aloud; another points out that the stated deadline conflicts with the way their support is scheduled. The shared goal remains clarity, but different conditions may require different approaches.

Ask about the experience relevant to the task. You can say, “What would make this explanation easier to use?” without asking someone to educate the group about an entire culture. When accounts differ, keep the differences visible. A person’s experience does not become false because another person had an easier time. Compare where the process worked, where it did not, and what information the team still needs before choosing a response.

inThisLesson: Identify when a broad statement hides relevant differences in experience.
Draft a respectful invitation for an individual perspective.
Choose a way to compare accounts without ranking people’s experiences.
Replace a generalization with an invitation to share relevant experience.
lessons.keyStatement: Find common purpose without erasing differences that affect participation.

items.title: Invite
items.body: Explain the decision and ask for the experience the person wants to share. Make declining or choosing another response method possible. An invitation is not a demand for personal disclosure.

items.title: Do not assign representation
items.body: One colleague or service user cannot supply every perspective within a community. Ask whose experience is still missing without treating identity as a qualification to speak for others.

items.title: Compare conditions
items.body: When accounts differ, examine context: the material used, timing, support, task, and available choices. This can reveal why a shared process has different effects without deciding one participant is wrong.

tabs.heading: Three ways to respond to a different experience

tabs.label: Flattening
tabs.body: We all use the same notice, so it should be equally clear to everyone. This treats a shared document as proof of a shared experience.

tabs.label: Curiosity
tabs.body: Which part was unclear, and what would make it more useful for you? This invites relevant detail without asking the person to defend their experience.

tabs.label: Adaptation
tabs.body: The team adds a concise summary and a clear contact option, then asks whether those changes help. It changes an approach and checks its usefulness.

check.question: Which invitation avoids making one person a representative of a whole group?
check.correct: Would you like to describe what made this notice easier or harder for you to use?
wrong: Tell us what everyone in your community thinks of the notice.
Confirm that your experience is the same as the majority’s.
Explain your cultural background before we consider your feedback.
check.feedbackCorrect: The question is relevant to the task and leaves the person in charge of what they share.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The alternatives demand representation, agreement, or personal disclosure before considering the feedback. Ask about the experience relevant to the notice instead.

sorting.heading: What kind of response is this?

items.text: The same email must work for everyone.
What helped you understand the action requested?
The team adds an optional phone response after checking the need.
Everyone knows what this term means.
Would another way of responding be more useful?
The team tests the revised instructions with willing participants.

lessons.next: Next, examine access and choice in how the notice can be used.

scenario.context: In this example, a colleague says a notice’s instructions assume people have someone nearby who can help. Another colleague replies that everyone needs support sometimes, so there is no difference to discuss.
scenario.prompt: What would help the team learn?
options: Acknowledge the shared need for support and ask which assumptions in the instructions may create a barrier.
Tell the first colleague their interpretation is too sensitive.
Label the second colleague’s IDI orientation in a personnel note.
responses: You retain common purpose while investigating a relevant difference. The team can examine the instructions rather than classify the people.
This dismisses a potentially useful observation before the team has examined it. Ask what the person noticed.
The program does not infer or record individual IDI orientations. Use the concepts to reflect on practice, not to create personnel labels.

lessons.transfer: Choose a familiar phrase such as “everyone knows.” What experience might it overlook, and what question could make room for that experience?

move.control: You can invite a perspective and reconsider an assumption in your own communication.
move.failure: A shared goal can be used to dismiss differences instead of understand them.
move.next: Ask one voluntary, task-specific question before finalizing a draft.

lessons.title: Offer usable ways to participate
lessons.summary: Plan access and check whether the options support the actual task.
lessons.objective: Identify an access barrier in a practice service notice.
objectives: Identify an access barrier in a practice service notice.
Compare a standard option with an alternative that addresses a stated barrier.
Choose a follow-up question that checks usability without collecting unnecessary personal information.
takeaways: An available document is not necessarily a usable document.
Ask about the task and the useful support rather than assuming a preference.
Check whether an alternative works; do not assume offering it solved the problem.
lessons.statement: Access means being able to receive, understand, and respond to information in a useful way.

image.caption: Service communication needs to work for the person using it.

intro.heading: Availability is only the beginning
intro.body:
In this example, a team posts its notice online and considers the task complete. A service user explains that they can find the file but cannot use its content with their reading technology. Another person understands the words but cannot tell which action is required. These are different concerns. Treating both as “the document is available” misses the actual task.

For communication disabilities, Department of Justice guidance explains that effective communication depends on the nature, length, complexity, and context of the interaction and the person’s usual method of communication. In practice, staff should use their agency’s access and accommodation processes rather than make a formal determination through a course exercise. The example here asks you to notice the concern and connect it to an appropriate response.

A better planning conversation asks what the recipient needs to accomplish: understand the change, compare options, ask a question, or make a response. Consider usable content, clear wording, a contact option, enough time, and a way to confirm understanding. No single alternative works for every person. Ask what is useful, work with the responsible staff, and check the result without requiring someone to disclose a diagnosis to the whole group.

inThisLesson: Identify an access barrier in a practice service notice.
Compare a standard option with an alternative that addresses a stated barrier.
Choose a follow-up question that checks usability without collecting unnecessary personal information.
Choose a response that addresses the stated task and preserves participation.
lessons.keyStatement: Ask whether the person can use the information, not only whether it was sent.

items.title: Receive
items.body: Check how information reaches the intended person. Posting something on a page does not tell you whether recipients know it is there or can obtain it.

items.title: Understand
items.body: Check wording, structure, format, and the action requested. Clear explanations and disability access are related, but one does not automatically establish the other.

items.title: Respond
items.body: Offer a clear route for questions and responses. Check whether the available route is useful and connect accommodation concerns to the designated process instead of improvising a legal decision.

tabs.label: Delivery
tabs.body: The notice was sent to the current contact list. This helps establish delivery work. It does not establish whether the notice was understood or usable.

tabs.label: Use
tabs.body: A willing participant explains the next step in their own words and identifies a confusing instruction. This provides specific feedback, not proof that everyone can use the notice.

tabs.label: Adjustment
tabs.body: The team revises the confusing instruction, checks the accessible format, and asks whether the change helped. Keep any unresolved issue visible and seek appropriate support.

check.question: A person can download a notice but cannot use its content. What is the most useful next step?
check.correct: Ask about the task and the barrier, and connect the concern to an appropriate usable format or communication support.
wrong: Count the download as proof that access was successful.
Ask the person to share a diagnosis with everyone at the meeting.
Assume any alternative file will solve the concern without checking.
check.feedbackCorrect: You focus on the actual use of the information and seek an appropriate response. The exercise does not decide which accommodation is legally required.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Downloading does not establish use, public diagnosis disclosure is unnecessary, and an untested alternative may leave the barrier in place.

sorting.heading: Which part of access is being examined?

items.text: Checking whether the contact address is current.
Explaining the action requested in familiar words.
Providing a clear route for questions.
Making the notice available through the agreed delivery method.
Checking whether the file works with the recipient’s reading technology.
Offering a useful way to confirm a choice.

lessons.next: Next, carry the observations into a proportionate change.

scenario.context: In a practice notice review, a participant requests a usable electronic version. The team is nearing its deadline. Someone suggests asking the participant to rely on a neighbor instead.
scenario.prompt: Which response best preserves access and agency?
options: Use the designated access process to arrange an appropriate version and check how the participant can contribute before the decision.
Tell the participant that personal assistance is always their responsibility.
Exclude the feedback because the deadline makes access inconvenient.
responses: You respond to the barrier without replacing the participant’s own contribution. Keep the decision timing and responsible process clear.
That assumes another person is available and that the arrangement is appropriate. It does not address the requested access.
A deadline does not make the access concern disappear. Raise the issue with the people responsible for the decision and the support.

lessons.transfer: Examine one message you help prepare. Can recipients tell what to do, obtain a usable version, ask a question, and make a response?

move.control: You can raise an access concern and involve the designated support before finalizing your part of the work.
move.failure: Treating distribution as success can hide a barrier to using the information.
move.next: Check one action in a notice from receiving it through responding to it.

lessons.title: Connect learning to a decision
lessons.summary: Compare options and explain a small change within your role.
lessons.objective: State the decision that remains open in a notice example.
objectives: State the decision that remains open in a notice example.
Compare two options using effects, evidence, and uncertainty.
Identify when a change needs another role’s authority or the required equity analysis process.
takeaways: A useful review starts with a decision that can still change.
Compare effects and uncertainties rather than declaring one option perfect.
Work within your authority and use the required agency process when it applies.
lessons.statement: An equity question becomes useful when it helps someone make or improve a decision.

image.caption: A draft can connect people’s experiences to a decision and its next step.

intro.heading: Turn observations into options
intro.body:
The practice team now has feedback on the notice. Participants found the instructions confusing, and the electronic format needs attention. The open decision is how to explain the change and collect contact preferences. Naming it prevents the review from becoming a broad conversation with no way to affect the work.

Compare options against the purpose. One option keeps the original notice and adds a contact number. Another revises the action statement, provides a usable format, and offers more than one response method. Consider who may benefit, what effort each option requires, what remains uncertain, and which evidence would help you choose. Do not label an option equitable simply because its intention sounds positive.

Your role matters. You may be able to improve wording in a draft, while another person controls the delivery method or decision timeline. State what you can change and what you need to raise. The DHS Equity Policy has required analysis procedures; this course’s reflection is not a replacement for them. A promising small change still needs the applicable review, authority, and follow-through. Keep those distinctions clear while developing a practical recommendation.

Compare two options using effects, evidence, and uncertainty.
Identify when a change needs another role’s authority or the required equity analysis process.
Compare two notice changes and identify the responsible next step.
lessons.keyStatement: Name the decision, compare effects, and keep responsibility visible.

items.title: Purpose
items.body: Explain what the notice should help people do. A clear purpose lets you compare options against the task instead of choosing the most polished-looking draft.

items.title: Effects
items.body: Consider likely benefits and barriers for different users, and state what supports each expectation. Include uncertainty. A convenient option for the team may shift effort to recipients.

items.title: Responsibility
items.body: Identify who can change the wording, format, timeline, and response process. Use the applicable equity analysis and review requirements rather than treating a learning note as approval.

tabs.label: Add a contact number
tabs.body: This may help people ask questions, but it leaves the original confusing action statement in place. Check the availability and usefulness of the contact route.

tabs.label: Revise the notice and response options
tabs.body: This addresses more than one identified barrier, but it requires editing, format work, and coordination. Check which concerns it actually resolves.

tabs.label: What remains uncertain?
tabs.body: The team has not yet tested the revised notice with willing users. Record that gap and arrange a proportionate check instead of claiming that the new version works for everyone.

check.question: Which recommendation is best supported by the example?
check.correct: Revise the identified confusing instruction and access issue, test the changes, and use the applicable review process before release.
wrong: Declare the new notice equitable because the team worked hard on it.
Skip the required review because this course already included reflection.
Make every possible change without considering the notice’s purpose or who can authorize it.
check.feedbackCorrect: The recommendation connects evidence to a specific response and leaves testing and responsibility visible.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Effort, course reflection, and the number of changes do not establish a sound decision. Connect the option to the barrier and use the appropriate review.

items.text: Recipients need to identify the action requested.
Several participants found the action statement unclear.
A revised opening may reduce that confusion.
A phone route could support questions but needs coverage.
The communications lead controls the release format.
The revised version has not yet been tested.

lessons.next: Next, plan how to learn from the change after it is used.

scenario.context: A practice analyst can revise the draft’s wording but cannot change the service response deadline. Feedback suggests both cause difficulty. A colleague asks the analyst to fix everything without involving anyone else.
scenario.prompt: What is a useful next step?
options: Improve the wording within the assignment and raise the deadline concern with the responsible decision maker, using the applicable review process.
Change the official deadline without authority because the intention is helpful.
Ignore the deadline concern because it falls outside the analyst’s immediate control.
responses: You act where you can and preserve the larger concern for the role that can address it. Responsibility supports action rather than becoming a reason to drop an issue.
A helpful intention does not grant authority to change an official condition. Raise the evidence and proposed option through the right process.
You can identify and refer a concern even when you cannot decide it. Record who needs to consider it and what information would help.

lessons.transfer: Name a decision in your current work that is still open. What can you change, what needs another role, and which evidence would help?

move.control: You can explain a barrier, compare options, and identify the next responsible role.
move.failure: A learning reflection can be mistaken for authority or approval if its limits are not clear.
move.next: Write a brief comparison of two options, including one uncertainty and the responsible next step.

lessons.title: Check what changed
lessons.summary: Distinguish completing an activity from improving someone’s opportunity to use a service.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a completed activity from evidence of a useful effect.
objectives: Distinguish a completed activity from evidence of a useful effect.
Choose a proportionate way to review the notice change.
Describe a result with its limits and a practical next adjustment.
takeaways: A revised notice is a completed activity, not proof of better access.
Use more than one kind of information when it helps answer the question.
Review can support another adjustment rather than a final success claim.
lessons.statement: Follow-through asks what people could do after the change, not only what the team produced.

image.caption: Reviewing a change can connect the finished notice to the experience of using it.

intro.heading: Learn from the next use
intro.body:
The practice team releases a revised notice. It is clearer, includes a usable version, and offers response choices. These are tangible changes. The team can accurately say what it produced. It still needs evidence before saying the notice improved access for everyone or eliminated a disparity.

Choose a question that matches the change. Did recipients understand the requested action? Were they able to use a response method? What concerns remained? A count of replies may help, but compare like periods and consider other changes that could affect the count. A few voluntary accounts may explain a confusing step; they do not measure the experience of every recipient. Combining information can help the team learn without overstating the result.

Keep the review proportionate and respectful. Use appropriate records and avoid collecting names, diagnoses, or sensitive details merely to make a learning exercise look thorough. Agree who will look at the information and when. If the response pattern improves while some people still report a barrier, keep both findings visible. A useful conclusion can be that the revision helped with one problem and that another step needs attention.

inThisLesson: Distinguish a completed activity from evidence of a useful effect.
Choose a proportionate way to review the notice change.
Describe a result with its limits and a practical next adjustment.
Write a result statement that separates activity, evidence, and uncertainty.
lessons.keyStatement: Say what changed, what supports your conclusion, and what remains unresolved.

items.title: Activity
items.body: The team revised the opening and added response choices. This establishes what was done. It does not establish how recipients experienced the result.

items.title: Observed effect
items.body: Willing readers could identify the requested action more easily in a small test. State the size and context of that test, and avoid generalizing it to every recipient.

items.title: Unresolved question
items.body: Some recipients still found the deadline difficult. Keep the concern visible and identify who can examine it. A positive finding elsewhere does not cancel it.

tabs.label: Overstatement
tabs.body: Our new notice eliminated access barriers. The team has not tested every relevant condition and cannot support that broad conclusion from a small review.

tabs.label: Useful finding
tabs.body: In a small voluntary review, participants identified the requested action more readily in the revised notice. Some still raised concerns about the deadline.

tabs.label: Next adjustment
tabs.body: The team retains the clearer wording, raises the deadline concern, and checks the response route again after the next release. This connects evidence to continued action.

check.question: Which statement keeps the result within the evidence?
check.correct: The team revised the notice; a small review suggests clearer action instructions, while the deadline concern remains unresolved.
wrong: Publishing a new notice proves equitable access.
A higher reply count proves the revision caused every improvement.
One unresolved concern means all parts of the revision were useless.
check.feedbackCorrect: You distinguish the activity, the limited evidence, and the remaining concern. That gives the team a useful basis for its next step.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The alternatives overstate success, assume causation, or erase useful progress. Keep findings and limitations together.

items.text: The team rewrote the action statement.
Several willing readers found the new opening clearer.
Can recipients use the response choices at the next release?
A usable electronic version was prepared.
Some readers still found the deadline difficult.
Who can review the deadline concern?

lessons.next: Use the job aid to apply the four ideas to one decision you help shape.

scenario.context: In this example, a team sees more replies after its notice change. It also changed the contact list and extended the response period. A manager wants to attribute the entire increase to clearer wording.
options: Report the increase and the other changes, explain that the cause is not isolated, and review which parts recipients found useful.
Credit the wording alone because it was the team’s preferred explanation.
Discard the count because it does not prove a single cause.
responses: You preserve useful information while keeping its limits clear. The review can help distinguish which changes mattered.
The result may reflect several changes. A preferred explanation is not evidence that the other conditions had no effect.
The count can still inform the review when its limits are stated. Lack of isolated causation does not make it worthless.

lessons.transfer: For one small change, write the activity completed, the effect you will examine, and a limit you should keep visible.

move.control: You can choose a review question and describe the result without overstating it.
move.failure: A finished product can be mistaken for proof that a barrier was removed.
move.next: Arrange a proportionate follow-up and choose whether to retain, revise, or raise the change after reviewing what happened.

jobAid.subtitle: Four ideas, one practical decision
remember: Name the task and the open decision.
Invite relevant perspectives without assigning representation.
Check whether people can receive, understand, and respond.
Compare options and use the applicable agency process.
Review what happened and state the limits.

sections.heading: Before the decision
items: Whose experience is present, and whose might be missing?
What condition could make the task harder?
What can still change, and who has responsibility?

sections.heading: After a change
items: What evidence suggests a useful effect?
What concern remains, and what should happen next?
